title: Trees, Not Tonnes: Survival-Linked Settlement for Smallholder Green Finance
content: A farmer records the mangroves she planted on the phone she already owns. The record is signed on the device and verifies offline, with no account and no network. She may publish it, and a viewer will draw her grove in three dimensions from what she reported, re-checking each record’s signature on the reader’s own machine and trusting no server for any of it. She may also anchor its hash to a permissioned chain, where a licensed commune agriculture officer who has ridden out and counted what is standing confirms or disputes it. Only that confirmation moves money: an escrowed sponsorship releases funds against the confirmed count, to the grower for the trees still alive and to the officer for the visit that established they were. One record therefore reaches two destinations of very different weight, and what each may carry differs accordingly. A picture and a payment are both wrappers around a claim. The picture may be wide — species, counts, photographs, even a carbon estimate — precisely because nothing depends on it; its only obligation is to avoid implying that something does. The payment must be narrow, because something does. The rule governing both is not ours: Holmström and Milgrom (1991) established that the power of an incentive should track the quality of the measure it is attached to, and that attaching a high-powered instrument to a poorly-measured outcome distorts what people do. We apply that result where it has not been applied — to the representation rather than the contract — and state it as a rule about artefacts: a representation may carry no claim stronger than the weakest link in the evidence that produced it, and the correct response to a weak claim is to shrink the wrapper rather than to strengthen the rhetoric. The voluntary carbon market inverted it, placing a counterfactual about an unobservable future inside a fungible and bridgeable instrument (Probst et al., 2024), and lost its credibility accordingly. Where consequences begin, therefore, this system records trees — a count somebody can walk out and falsify, to which a person holding a licence they can lose has put their name. The carbon figure survives in the diary and in the picture, labelled with the model that produced it; it does not cross onto the chain, and nothing is minted against it. We describe an implementation spanning three public repositories and show that its interesting output is what it refuses: payment is withheld against a photograph older than the promise, against a record nobody has confirmed, and against a confirmation any single licensed verifier has disputed. Token supply falls when trees die, and the registry contains no path by which an issuer may choose it — though, as Section 5 reports, the token’s role hierarchy leaves one open that the registry’s logic does not. The loop this closes runs from the physical world to the digital and back, and its return path is a payment rather than a control signal. By the prevailing taxonomy, which grades digital twins by how automated their data flows are, a farmer photographing her trees makes this a digital model — the weakest category available. We accept the classification and dispute the criterion, and propose an accountability axis orthogonal to it: what makes a representation worth acting upon is not how automatically it updates but who bears the cost of its being wrong. We give a per-layer account of what each mechanism does and does not establish, report a defect and a mis-attribution found in our own system while writing, and are explicit that the oracle problem is neither solved nor solvable here. This is a design paper and contains no empirical content. Nothing described has been deployed, no grower has used it, no verifier has been licensed, and the evaluation protocol we specify has not been run. Where we report that code does something, we have executed it; that establishes what the code does and nothing about whether the design works.
